items.content: <article>[This is a Guest Diary by Kevin Truong, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]</article>

items.title: Java4Shell, NGINX2Shell and more: Why we are not at "Yellow", (Wed, Nov 18th)
items.content: <article>About a month ago, we went to Infocon Yellow for the first time in a few years. We decided to address the php2shell vulnerability and alert our readers to its significant impact. Following php2shell, we had a number of vulnerabilities and events that may also have scored high enough to trigger an Infocon "Yellow" [infocon]. In the last few days, we had a major Microsoft 365 outage, a critical vulnerability in Java, and a critical vulnerability in NGINX, which was disclosed today.</article>

A phishing page interested in MX records, (Tue, Nov 17th)
items.content: <article>I’ve mentioned before in some of my diaries that it can be instructive to look at what appear to be “generic” phishing messages in detail from time to time, since some of them might prove not to be as generic as they initially appear. I came across a good example of this while going over phishing messages delivered to our handler inbox over the past few weeks, when a message that, at first glance, appeared to be a fairly ordinary attempt at stealing e-mail credentials turned out to lead to a page interested in collecting a little more information than just the victim's password.</article>

Scans for LiteLLM/Starlette (CVE-2026-42271, CVE-2026-48710), (Mon, Nov 16th)
items.content: <article>This weekend, we started seeing requests for /mcp-rest/test/tools/list hitting our honeypots. These requests appear to attempt to exploit CVE-2026-42271 and CVE-2026-48710. Horizon3.ai published a short write-up about how these vulnerabilities can be chained to achieve remote code execution without authentication [Horizon3]</article>
